source_title: Civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Ukraine-held territory
source_excerpt:
Their evacuation is part of a major rescue operation carried out under a six-day ceasefire
Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have crossed into Ukrainian-held territory after a humanitarian mission and localized ceasefire.
"As of now, Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region. All of them will receive the assistance they need," said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, thanking the U.S. and Melania Trump for mediation.
Ukrainian officials greeted the evacuees with posters reading "You're not alone" and "We embrace with our hearts."
The residents travelled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus. The crossing took place under restrictions imposed by Ukrainian authorities that did not permit the disclosure of the number of evacuees or the location of the border crossing.
Ukrainian organizers said the restrictions were imposed in part to safeguard residents who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect the safety of similar humanitarian missions that may occur.
Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Ukraine-held territory
It was a rare joint Russia-Ukraine humanitarian effort — a brief respite in the grim war. The ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region began at 3 a.m. local time Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
Civilians from Oleshky, on the Dnipro River, began the long journey out of the war-ravaged region in bus convoys on Friday. The estimated 2,000 remaining residents were offered the choice of travelling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
A resident evacuated from from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky reacts while being flanked by his daughter and wife, who were waiting to welcome him, as he returns to Ukrainian-controlled territory, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, at an undisclosed location on Saturday. (Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters)
Supply routes to Oleshky have been disrupted by fighting and drones. According to some residents, food deliveries were stopped in May, pushing hundreds of people into starvation.
Russia's Ministry of Defence said those who chose to travel from Oleshky to Ukrainian-held territory were taken to the Russian city of Anapa and flown to the Belarusian city of Homel. They were accompanied by Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's commissioner for human rights, it said.
Daughters wait to see their fathers again
Relatives waited on Saturday at the border between Ukraine and Belarus, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them.
Volunteers from organizations, including the Red Cross, Doctors without Borders and the World Central Kitchen, were also there.

Aid operation, evacuations underway in Ukraine's stricken city of Oleshky
Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father more than two years ago, was among those waiting. Paliy, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory at the time, while he stayed behind.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
U.S.-brokered ceasefire begins in Russian-occupied Ukrainian town
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbours but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realized that, well, there was no [other] way, and he walked us to the road and that was it," Pavlyn said of the last time she saw her father.

She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.
Russia's ombudsperson and lead representative on the mission, Yana Lantratova, said buses also transported Oleshky residents who wanted to live in Russia. Russian media outlets on Saturday showed civilians arriving at a temporary accommodation site in Simferopol on the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
Two evacuees wearing Ukrainian flags feed their cat after arriving at an undisclosed location on Ukrainian-controlled territory on Saturday. (Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters)
Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
A video shared by Ukraine's ombudsman showed dozens of Oleshky residents slowly disembarking from a plane at a Belarusian airfield. Many people were elderly. Some required help to walk, and a few were carried on stretchers or in wheelchairs. They carried minimal luggage — only a bag or two. Dogs were unloaded from the plane in cages.
As several big buses crossed into Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region from Belarus, the residents were greeted by relatives. Ambulances lined the street and several large military tents were erected where hot meals, tea and medical aid were provided.
Animals were among those who made the journey on Saturday, with Ukrainian emergency services, Red Cross and UAnimals NGO employees handling the pets of residents evacuated from Oleshky into Ukrainian-held territory. (Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters)
Pet food and water bottles were piled up on several tables.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
U.S. approves Patriot missile sales for Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday welcomed U.S. approval of Ukraine’s purchase of 500 PAC-3 Patriot interceptors but urged partners to supply the weapons from existing stocks to protect the country this winter, warning the newly authorized U.S. sale could take years to deliver.
"Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day. In just these past two weeks of October, there have already been more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of our power grid," Zelenskyy wrote on X.
24 hours in Kyiv: Living through Russian drone strikes
The Trump administration said Friday that it had approved a proposed $2.1 billion US sale of Patriot air defence interceptors, after Kyiv had accused the Pentagon of delaying deliveries of the vital munition needed to stop Russian ballistic missiles.
The U.S. State Department said 500 Patriot missiles would be purchased for Ukraine with donations from Canada, Germany and Norway through a U.S. program and that no American funds were involved.
A Ukrainian drone attack kills 2 in Russia
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.
Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.

Russia's Ministry of Defence said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.
The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.

Zelenskyy urged partners to impose further sanctions on Russia and provide new support packages to Ukraine.
"The world sees Russia targeting civilian infrastructure every day. Everyone who does not want to see this Russian escalation spread further into Europe must help Ukraine," he said in an online post.
